reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later boards reviewed. Begin after ...Bxc4 at 140 seconds in the complete nine-piece source variation. c8=Q+ is proved through all legal replies to actual mate, retaining a5/b5/b4, Rc1, Bc4 and g7. The bishop blocks its own rook from capturing on c8. The preceding ten-piece c7/Rc1/Be2+ plan, pawn-capture branch and separate rook-capture branch remain outside this selected proof; those larger branches are not certified merely by their promotion claims.
transcript: The white king is really in trouble. The light-squared bishop is hanging and black is already up six points of material. If white tries to save the bishop and defend his pawn at the same time, now the other pawn is going to fall and we have no progress to make. Not only that, the other pawn is hanging, too. So, how can white make any progress in this position? [music] Well, you see, white is not only able to make progress, but white is actually completely winning. And it all starts with pawn to c7. This is threatening to get a new queen in just one move. If black takes the bishop, this is going to be a fork picking up the rook right [music] away and winning the game. So, black cannot allow that and instead after c7, he plays rook to c1. Now preparing to sacrifice the rook for the newly born queen and that would still be enough for black to win. If white tries to get a queen, now after rook takes and king takes, bishop to b3 is going to defend the promotion square of the other pawn and having three pawns, black is going to win. But white has other ideas in mind and instead of promoting the pawn right away, plays bishop to e2 check. Black has two ways of covering this check. If he covers with the bishop, now the g pawn is going to run to promotion and there is no way of stopping both pawns. So, white is going to get a queen, get a second queen and this would be completely winning [music] for white. But what would happen if black had defended with a pawn? Well, again, white can play pawn to g7, but this time it's different. After bishop to b3, both of the promotion squares are defended by the black pieces and it seems like white is just going to lose. And indeed, this would be winning for black in every universe out there. But not in this one. Because white has the majestic and incredible bishop to c4. A move that looks like the most outrageous blunder that white could play in this [music] position. The bishop is hanging three different ways, but the key idea behind this move is the fact that if the pawn takes, white is going to be able to promote with check and then promote the other pawn and have two queens winning the game. But if the bishop takes, again, we can promote the C pawn with a check and actually this time this is going to lead to a checkmate. But if the rook takes, now the G pawn is going to promote >> [music] >> and not only that, this is a threat of a checkmate in one move. So black has to cover that, but now the other pawn promotes. Black takes and after this, black is going to get checkmated very soon.
